SpriteForge makes custom pixel art usable in games that cannot load image files. Each sprite is stored as a short list of coloured rectangles; a small runtime (pix.lua) draws those rectangles as plain UI image controls. The result looks like a normal sprite and can be moved, scaled, tinted and animated.

It was built for Miliastra Wonderland (Genshin Impact UGC) Lua client scripts, where creators have no way to upload textures, but the format is engine-neutral: anything that can draw a coloured rectangle can draw a SpriteForge sprite.

Draw on the grid, or Import a picture: it is shrunk to the grid size and reduced to a few colours. The red cross is the anchor: the point that sits at the x,y you give in code (usually the feet or the centre). Keep sprites small: 12-32 pixels is typical; each extra colour or stray pixel adds rectangles.

The number next to each sprite is its cost in rectangles. Every rectangle is one UI control in the game, so fewer is faster. A clean 16×16 character costs 20-40; a photo quantised to 16 colours can cost 300+.

Colours are keys (names) with a value in the base palette. Keys p0-p3 and q0-q3 are tint slots: a variant palette (blue, gold, team2…) replaces only those keys. In the game you choose the variant when you place the sprite, so one drawing becomes many colour versions for free.
Double-click a colour to edit it. Use Presets for a quick starter palette. Alpha below 255 makes a translucent colour, which costs more rectangles - use it sparingly.
Layers stack bottom to top. Tick 'part' on a layer to export it separately (sprite/layer): the game can then show or hide it (a hat, a label, a glow) or a state can switch it on and off.

Frames are drawings; a clip is what moves. A clip changes position, scale, rotation, opacity, the current frame or the colour variant over time. Looping clips (idle, float) run forever; one-shot clips (hit, pop, fadeout) end and fire an 'end' event. Try a Preset, press Space, then change a key value to see what it does.

A behaviour is a set of states. Each state plays a clip and chooses a variant and parts. Rules switch between states: on an event the game sends ('tap'), after a random delay, when the clip ends, or when a number crosses a threshold (hp < 0.2). The game code stays tiny: actor:fire('tap'), actor:set('hp', 0.2).

pix.lua is the runtime for Miliastra Wonderland Lua client scripts (editor 7.1+). Other engines can read the same pixdata.lua: the format is described in the Docs.

Put the three files into the external_lua_file folder of your stage. To find it: Client Script Resource Explorer → right-click → New Client Script, then copy the path from the address bar of the folder window.
Client Script Resource Explorer → right-click → Batch Add Script Files → Add by Folder. A file without a mapping never reaches the game.

Manage UI Control Groups → Interface Layout → Add UI Control → Client Control Container. Name it PX_Root, then Canvas Settings → Go to Edit. In code, (0, 0) is the centre of this container; the canvas is 1600×900.
UI Control Group Library → Client Control Templates → new template of type Image. Write down its Control Template Index ID.
On PX_Root: Script tab → Add Script → spriteforge_main.lua. Attach only this file; it loads pix and pixdata by itself.
Right-click spriteforge_main.lua → Edit Script Variables → add a variable:
At the top of spriteforge_main.lua: SPRITE is the sprite name exactly as on its tab, SIZE is how many screen units one pixel takes. The file downloaded from here already has the current sprite.

Ctrl+S, restart the Sandbox completely, Test Play. Logs → Client Scripts should show "SpriteForge: <name> ready". "no container or TPL_SPRITE" means the variable from step 6 is missing or has the wrong index.
After redrawing: export pixdata.lua again, replace the file, Ctrl+S and restart the Sandbox. Mappings and editor settings stay.

There are two kinds of animation, and they work together.
Frames are different drawings of the same sprite, like pages of a flip-book. You draw them in Draw, in the strip under the canvas; the play button there only previews them.

Clips are movement over time, made in Animate: position, stretch, rotation, opacity, which frame is shown and the colour variant. A clip can contain a 'frame' track, so the flip-book becomes part of the clip. + Clip from frames makes such a clip in one click.
Make the clips first (Animate): for example idle, pop and drain.
Open Behave and press Create behaviour. It starts with one state, idle.
Add a state for every situation with + State (pop, empty, gone…). For each state choose its clip, colour variant and which parts are shown.
Under Switch to another state… add rules: on event (the game calls actor:fire), when the clip ends, after a random delay, when a number is below or above a value (the game calls actor:set).
Add the numbers the rules use with + Number, then test with the buttons and sliders under Preview.

Besides pixel art, a sprite can be a drawing: brush strokes, lines, circles and boxes. Choose Drawing in New sprite…. It is still a normal sprite: colours and variants, layers and parts, frames, clips and behaviours work exactly the same.

In the game every stroke is rebuilt from rectangles and circles with the same positions, sizes and angles as in the editor, so it looks identical at any size. The cost is the number of these pieces: about two per corner of a stroke. Smoothing removes corners.
Brush (B): hold the mouse button and draw. Width and Smoothing are above the canvas. The right button draws with the secondary colour.
Line (L), Rectangle (U), Ellipse (C): drag from corner to corner. Filled makes a solid shape, otherwise you get an outline of the chosen width. Shift keeps lines at 45° and makes squares and circles.
Select and move (V): click a shape and drag it. Above the canvas: To front, To back, Duplicate, Delete. Arrow keys with Shift nudge it.
Eraser (E) deletes whole shapes, Recolour (G) gives a shape the primary colour, Pick colour (I) takes a shape's colour. Mirror draws a mirrored copy of every new shape.
Everything else is the same as for pixel sprites: layers, frames, Animate, Behave, Export.
